nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits, lowest bit first), the cost of incrementing $b$ is at most $k$.
nodes.title: Increment costs at most the width

nodes.summary: For every $k$, the cost of incrementing the $k$-bit counter whose $k$ bits are all $1$ is exactly $k$.
nodes.title: Incrementing the all-ones counter costs the full width

nodes.summary: Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter stored lowest bit first, and let $t$ be the length of its initial run of $1$ bits, that is, the largest $t \le k$ with $b_0 = \dots = b_{t-1} = 1$. The cost of incrementing $b$ is $t + 1$ if $t < k$, and $t$ if $t = k$.
nodes.title: Exact cost of an increment

nodes.summary: Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter stored lowest bit first, with bits $b_i \in \{0, 1\}$ and unsigned value $v(b) = \sum_{i < k} b_i 2^i$. If $b'$ is the counter returned by incrementing $b$, then $v(b') = (v(b) + 1) \bmod 2^k$.
nodes.title: Increment adds one with wraparound

nodes.summary: A $k$-bit counter is a vector $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ of bits stored lowest bit first. Incrementing $b$ changes the initial run of $1$ bits $b_0, \dots, b_{t-1}$ to $0$ and then changes the first $0$ bit $b_t$, if there is one, to $1$; if every bit is $1$, all bits become $0$ and no new bit is added. The result is again a $k$-bit counter, and the cost of the increment is the number of bits changed, one unit per…
nodes.title: Binary counter increment

nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits), the cost of resetting $b$ plus the number of $1$ bits in the returned counter equals the number of $1$ bits in $b$.
nodes.title: Potential identity for reset

nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$, resetting the counter returned by resetting $b$ returns the same counter as resetting $b$ once.
nodes.title: Reset is idempotent

nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$, resetting the counter returned by resetting $b$ has cost $0$.
nodes.title: A second reset costs nothing

nodes.summary: Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter and $b' = (b'_0, \dots, b'_{k-1})$ the counter returned by resetting $b$. The cost of resetting $b$ equals the number of indices $i < k$ with $b_i \ne b'_i$.
nodes.title: Reset cost is the Hamming distance

nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits), the cost of resetting $b$ is at most $k$.
nodes.title: Reset costs at most the width

nodes.summary: For every width $k$, resetting the all-false bit vector of width $k$ has cost $0$.
nodes.title: Resetting the all-false counter costs nothing

nodes.summary: Resetting a bit vector of width $0$ has cost $0$.
nodes.title: Resetting a width-zero counter costs nothing

nodes.summary: For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the cost of resetting $b$ equals the number of positions of $b$ that hold true.
nodes.title: Cost of resetting a binary counter

nodes.summary: For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the bits returned by resetting $b$ are, in order, $k$ copies of false.
nodes.title: Reset returns the all-false counter

nodes.summary: For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the bits returned by resetting $b$, read low-order bit first as an unsigned binary numeral, have value $0$.
nodes.title: Reset yields the value zero

nodes.summary: Resetting a bit vector $b$ of width $k$ returns the all-false bit vector of width $k$ and charges cost $1$ for each position of $b$ that holds true, that is, for each bit it changes from true to false.
nodes.title: Resetting a binary counter

nodes.summary: Let $k$, $i$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $i < k$, and for each $t$ let $c_t$ be the bit vector returned by running $t$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$. Then the number of $t < n$ such that the bit at position $i$ of $c_t$ (counting from the low-order bit, starting at $0$) differs from the bit at position $i$ of $c_{t+1}$ is $\lfloor n / 2^i \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Flip counts of the individual bits

nodes.summary: For every bit vector $b$ and every natural number $n$, the bit vector returned by running $n + 1$ increments from $b$ is the increment of the bit vector returned by running $n$ increments from $b$.
nodes.title: One more increment

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$, running $n$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$ costs exactly $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \lfloor n / 2^i \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Exact cost of increments from zero

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$ with $k > 0$, running $n$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$ costs at least $n$.
nodes.title: Lower bound on the cost of increments from zero

nodes.summary: For every width $k$ and every $n > 0$, performing $n$ successive increments on the $k$-bit counter that starts with all bits zero costs strictly fewer than $2n$ bit changes in total.
nodes.title: Aggregate cost bound for the binary counter

nodes.summary: For every width $k$, every $k$-bit counter $b$ and every $n$, the cost of running $n + 1$ successive increments from $b$ equals the cost of running $n$ increments from $b$ plus the cost of incrementing the counter that the $n$-step run returns.
nodes.title: Cost recurrence for the binary counter run

nodes.summary: For every width $k$, every $k$-bit counter $b$ and every $n$, let $v$ be the value of $b$ read as an unsigned binary number with the least significant bit first. After $n$ successive increments starting from $b$, the counter read the same way has value $(v + n) \bmod 2^k$.
nodes.title: Counter value after successive increments

nodes.summary: For every width $k$ and every $k$-bit counter $b$, running zero increments from $b$ returns $b$ unchanged at cost zero.
nodes.title: Running zero increments

nodes.summary: For a width $k$, a $k$-bit counter $b$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the run of $n$ increments from $b$ is defined recursively. The run of $0$ increments returns $b$ at cost zero. The run of $n + 1$ increments performs the run of $n$ increments, then increments the counter it returned and returns the result; its cost is the cost of the $n$-step run plus the cost of that increment.
nodes.title: Running the binary counter

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
